score_justification: L3 LLM summarises reviews and lease clauses; E3 UGC + moderation + defamation workflow takes weeks; A4 strong renter search intent; P3 SEO on address/landlord-name queries; M4 address-level landlord behaviour history compounds; W2 landlords resist paying; renters pay little
unique_data_capture: Address- and LLC-level ledger of deposit-return outcomes, repair response times and lease-clause terms, linked across shell companies via county property records; each review strengthens owner-entity matching.
commoditization_risk: Medium: Google Maps and apartment sites carry building reviews, but not owner-entity history across properties.

fix.problem: Renters sign 12-month leases with almost no way to research the landlord or management company behind a building. Problems with deposits, ignored repairs and harassment usually surface only after move-in, when leaving is expensive. Building-level reviews exist, but owners hide behind LLCs and property managers, so a bad operator's record does not follow them from building to building.
fix.solution: An address-searchable directory of landlord and management-company reviews that links buildings to their owning entity using county assessor and LLC registry data. Renters rate repair response time, deposit return, lease fairness and communication, and upload a lease or utility bill to get a verified-tenant badge. An LLM summary turns many reviews into a short pros and cons card per owner. Landlords can claim a profile and respond publicly. Unlike building-only review sites, a bad operator's history follows them across every property they own.

The same procedure can cost several times more across clinics in one city (est.). Clinics do not publish prices, and review sites rate bedside manner, not cost.
fix.solution: A vet price directory built from owner-submitted invoices. An OCR and LLM pipeline turns photographed receipts into standard procedure line items with clinic, date and ZIP. Owners search a procedure and see median and range prices by clinic, plus whether the clinic belongs to a corporate chain. Price alerts flag when a clinic's prices jump. Clinics can claim profiles and post a price list to earn a transparency badge, so owners get an estimate before booking.

Unlicensed or unpermitted jobs, abandoned projects and change-order surprises are common complaints. Lead-gen sites sell the same lead to several contractors, so the platform has little reason to verify quality.
fix.solution: A contractor directory where every review is tied to a verified project: before and after photos, the municipal permit number pulled from city open-data portals, job type and approximate cost. A vision model tags photos by trade and finish quality, and licence and insurance status is checked against state boards. Homeowners filter by project type and see each contractor's permitted job history. Contractors pay a flat subscription rather than per lead, so the directory stays independent.

Fees vary widely and are rarely posted. Older notary directories list commissions but not availability, specialties such as loan signings or apostille, or verified insurance.
fix.solution: A mobile notary directory with live availability, posted travel and signing fees, and specialties such as loan signing, hospital visits, jail visits, apostille and bilingual service. Each profile is checked against the state commission database and shows E&O insurance and NNA certification. Customers book and pay through the site, and notaries pay a booking fee or subscription. It also flags when remote online notarization is allowed for the document, so users choose the cheapest valid option.

State licensing agencies publish inspection and violation reports, but they sit in hard-to-search PDFs that vary by state. Serious citations, such as ratio violations, unsafe sleep and abuse findings, are mixed in with paperwork lapses. Most parents decide on a tour and a few online reviews.
fix.solution: A daycare directory that ingests state licensing inspection reports and uses an LLM to classify each citation by severity and category, from paperwork to supervision to safety. Every provider shows a plain-English violation timeline, its repeat-violation pattern, staff ratios, openings and tuition ranges. Parent reviews come from verified enrolled families. Alerts tell subscribed parents when a new inspection is posted, and providers can claim profiles to post openings and responses.

Inspection reports and staffing data exist but are scattered across CMS and 50 state agencies.
fix.solution: An independent senior-care directory that merges CMS Care Compare ratings, staffing levels and inspection citations with state assisted-living records and verified family reviews. An LLM writes a plain-English risk summary for each facility and flags recent serious citations. Families filter by care level, Medicaid acceptance, memory-care capability and reported monthly price. Facilities pay for enhanced profiles, not placement fees, and the site says so clearly. The result is a neutral view that referral-fee sites cannot offer.

Couples see real price ranges by category and region before contacting anyone. Reviews can be updated six months later, when photo delivery delays and issues surface. Vendors pay a flat listing fee with no pay-to-rank, and the ranking method is published.

Funeral homes must give an itemised price list on request under the FTC Funeral Rule, but many still do not post prices online. Costs for the same service can differ several-fold in one city, and corporate owners often keep local family names.
fix.solution: A funeral price directory that collects General Price Lists from websites and mystery-shopper requests, then uses an LLM to extract each line item into a standard format. Families compare direct cremation, burial packages, embalming and casket prices, and see the corporate owner behind each home. A price-history view shows increases over time. Homes that post full prices online earn a transparency badge and can pay for a premium profile.

Plumbers update availability by SMS or a simple app toggle, and licences are verified against state boards. After each job, customers report the quoted and final price. Plumbers pay per completed booking, not per lead, which keeps the listings honest.

Owners filter by breed, size, temperament handling, such as anxious or reactive dogs, and services such as hand-stripping or cat grooming. Each listing shows price ranges by breed and size. Groomers can claim profiles and add portfolios, and owners can book through links to the groomer's own booking tool.

An intake questionnaire with an LLM summary suggests three matches with confirmed openings and insurance. Clients give optional, private feedback after session four, which improves future matches. Therapists pay a monthly listing fee similar to existing directories.

fix.solution: A lawyer directory organised by sub-specialty and case type, such as non-compete disputes or guardianship. Experience is backed by public court docket counts where available, plus bar status and discipline history. Users describe their problem in plain language and an LLM maps it to the right sub-specialty without giving legal advice. Lawyers pay a flat profile subscription, which complies with advertising rules, and can list fee structures and free-consult policies.

General directories list accountants by location only. Owners often discover a bad fit at tax time, after a costly mistake.

CPA licences are verified against state boards, and software certifications such as QuickBooks ProAdvisor and Xero are listed. Firms describe their typical client and show sample engagements. Firms pay for featured profiles, and the site earns affiliate fees from accounting software.

Practices can claim profiles and post new-patient availability, and the site earns money from appointment booking integrations.

Profiles show fiduciary status, compensation type, conflicts and disciplinary history. Users filter by fee-only, flat-fee, minimums and specialties such as equity compensation or retirement planning. Advisors pay for enhanced profiles, while the fee data stays free and neutral.

Revenue comes from affiliate links and sponsorships. As of 2026 this is crowded and AI assistants answer these questions directly, so it is not recommended.
